paras: The lynching of John Wagoner took place shortly after midnight on the night of January 19, 1882, when a band of forty to sixty masked men took him from the Lawrence County jail at Ironton, Ohio, and hanged him from a tree in the court house yard. Wagoner was awaiting trial for the November 1881 killing of Dr. Joseph A. Beggs; his co-defendant, William Zeek, was also taken out and threatened with the rope, and confessed before being returned to his cell. The case drew attention as the first lynching in the county's history and as the second in Ohio in a short time, and Ohio papers divided over whether it was justified.

Dr. Beggs, bookkeeper and chemist at the Etna Iron Works, was shot late at night in late November 1881 just east of Ironton, and John Wagoner and Bill Zeek were named as his killers. At the coroner's inquest the accused and others testified that a man calling himself "Old Hell" had kicked at the fence of Wagoner's house and was shot when he would not leave, but the Jackson Standard noted other evidence placing the killing on the railroad. After a preliminary examination before Mayor Corns, both men were committed without bail on a charge of first-degree murder.

Citizens of Ironton met and asked Judge Harper to hold a special term of court for the trial, and raised money for Beggs's widow and children. An Ironton correspondent of the Cincinnati Commercial wrote that there had been many threats of lynching, because so many murderers in the area had gone unhanged through "the stupidity and rascality of jurors."

Shortly after twelve o'clock a knock brought Sheriff Kimball to the jail door, where masked men seized him and held cocked revolvers to his head while demanding the keys. When he refused, ten or fifteen of them marched him to his room and repeated the demand, and his frightened wife told them where the keys were. The band opened the cell holding Wagoner and Zeek and led both men out.

According to the Eaton Democrat, Wagoner protested, "I didn't mean to kill him," and within two minutes was hanging from a tree a few feet from the court house. Zeek, swung up or held with a rope around his neck, confessed and implicated others, after which he was locked back in his cell. Guards posted around the yard held passers-by until the work was done, and the band then dispersed in all directions. The body hung until morning, when the coroner viewed it and cut it down.

On the strength of Zeek's confession, Mrs. Zeek and a Mrs. Hall were arrested the next morning. By January 31 no one had been arrested for the lynching, and Mrs. Zeek and a man named Marshall had been discharged because Zeek refused to make a sworn statement against them. Across the Ohio River at Catlettsburg, Kentucky, guards over the prisoners in the Ashland murder trial were said to have kept the strictest watch since the Ironton lynching. No report of an inquest verdict, an indictment or a trial of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The story went out on January 20 in Cincinnati dispatches, a Times-Star special reporting that the masked men had "dispatched Wagoner" and that "public opinion apparently approves the act." Versions of this wire ran from Savannah and Marietta to Los Angeles and St. Paul, often with the murdered man's name garbled as Briggs or Biggs and Zeek's as Seek, while news summaries reduced it to a single line. The Memphis Public Ledger headed its first dispatch "Plantation Manners in Ohio" and later, quoting the Commercial's account of a drilled band with numbers and squad captains, judged that Wagoner "no doubt, deserved hanging, but the mob had no more right" than any other.

Ohio papers split along the lines the Spirit of Democracy described, with some giving "encouragement" to mob law. The Jackson Standard declared "that this was right" and reprinted an Ironton Bee editorial calling for the abolition of juries. The Stark County Democrat called the lynching "all wrong as long as the law may operate," and the Spirit of Democracy tied it to the unpunished lynching of Davis in Athens County. As far away as Washington Territory, the Vancouver Independent said the people had acted because they feared the courts would not do justice.
No article in the coverage states the race of Wagoner or Zeek, and the Eaton Democrat described Wagoner as having "mild blue eyes."

The Cincinnati wire said Zeek was swung up first and Wagoner hanged afterward, while the Eaton Democrat put Wagoner's hanging first and Zeek's confession after it. Accounts of the confession differ: the Eaton Democrat and Jackson Standard said Zeek named Wagoner as the shooter, while the Globe's Ironton dispatch had him say Beggs was killed by Sarah Zeck, Wagoner or Frank Marshall for a single silver dollar. Most reports place the lynching on Thursday night, January 19, but the Memphis Public Ledger and the Marietta Journal call it Friday night.

accounts.label: Cincinnati wire (Times-Star special)
accounts.gist: Forty to sixty masked men took both prisoners out between twelve and one; Zeek was swung up first and confessed, then Wagoner was hanged; no clue to the perpetrators.

accounts.label: Ironton dispatch (Globe)
accounts.gist: A well-organized band took Wagoner; Zeck, with a rope around his neck, confessed an organized murder-and-robbery band and said Beggs was killed by Sarah Zeck, Wagoner or Frank Marshall.

accounts.label: Ohio narrative (Eaton Democrat, Democratic Northwest)
accounts.gist: The sheriff was seized at the door and his wife gave up the keys; Wagoner was hanged within two minutes, then the terrified Zeek confessed that Wagoner did the killing.

accounts.label: Cincinnati Commercial special
accounts.gist: Described the lynching as the county's first, done by a disciplined, numbered band of forty or fifty provoked by unpunished murders.

framing.detail: The Memphis Public Ledger headlined the first dispatch 'Plantation Manners in Ohio' and later said the man 'no doubt, deserved hanging' but the mob had no right.
The Jackson Standard said 'this was right' and wanted lynch law extended to judges and jurors.
The Stark County Democrat and Spirit of Democracy called it wrong while the law could operate.
The Vancouver Independent said the people had good reason to fear the courts.
Most papers ran the Cincinnati wire or a one-line summary.
